tips.title: Genotype is the alleles, phenotype is the appearance
tips.body: **Genotype** is the **alleles** an organism has — `Bb`. **Phenotype** is the **characteristic you can observe** — brown eyes. Two different genotypes, `BB` and `Bb`, can give the **same** phenotype, which is the whole reason recessive traits can reappear.

tips.title: Heterozygous × heterozygous gives 3 : 1
tips.body: `Bb × Bb` always gives **1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb**, which is a **3 : 1** phenotype ratio — **75%** dominant and **25%** recessive. Recognising this cross saves drawing the square under time pressure.

tips.title: Homozygous is the same, heterozygous is different
tips.body: **Homo** means same — `BB` or `bb`, two identical alleles. **Hetero** means different — `Bb`. Only a **homozygous recessive** (`bb`) shows a recessive characteristic, because one dominant allele is enough to mask it.

tips.title: Label the Punnett square before filling it
tips.body: Write the **parent genotypes**, then their **gametes** along the top and side, then fill the boxes. Labelling first is what prevents the commonest error — combining two alleles from the **same** parent.

tips.title: Each child is an independent 25% or 50%
tips.body: A ratio is a **probability for each birth**, not a guarantee across a family. Parents who already have three children with a condition still face the **same** chance with the fourth — the previous births change nothing.

why.matters:
A Punnett square is four boxes, and it turns a question about a family into arithmetic. That is the whole reason genetics became a science: the outcomes are not a matter of opinion, they are counted.

What the square gives you is a **probability**, not a promise. Four boxes means the chance at each conception, not the four children a family will have — and keeping those apart is where most of the marks in this topic are.

examples.title: Why two people with no condition can have a child who has one
examples.body:
If both parents carry one recessive allele and one dominant one, neither shows the condition — one working copy is enough. Their gametes are another matter.

The square has **4** boxes: one FF, two Ff, one **ff**. So there is a **1-in-4 chance** at each conception that the child inherits the recessive allele from both, and 2 in 4 that they are a carrier like their parents. Nothing new appeared; the allele was there all along, hidden by the other one.

props.title: Two carriers: 1 FF, 2 Ff, 1 ff — a 1 in 4 chance

visual.alt: A Punnett square for two carriers, each with one dominant and one recessive allele, giving one FF, two Ff and one ff: a one in four chance that a child inherits the recessive allele from both parents

examples.title: Why a family of four girls says nothing about the fifth
examples.body:
Sex is decided by which sperm arrives: an egg always carries an X, and a sperm carries X or Y. The square gives two XX and two XY, so the chance is **a half**, every time.

And the square is redrawn from scratch at every conception. Four girls already born do not change the next one, because nothing carries over — the same mistake as expecting a coin to even out. A probability of a half means half of many, not alternating.

props.title: Two XX and two XY: a 50% chance at every conception

visual.alt: A Punnett square for sex determination: the mother contributes an X either way and the father an X or a Y, giving two XX and two XY, a fifty per cent chance at every conception

examples.title: Why genotype and phenotype are not the same word
examples.body:
The **genotype** is the pair of alleles; the **phenotype** is what you can observe. Two of the four boxes above have different genotypes and the same phenotype, which is exactly why the distinction is needed.

It is also why a recessive allele can travel through generations unseen. Nobody in a family shows a condition, everyone assumes it is not there, and it appears when two carriers happen to have a child together. An answer that says *they have the gene* has confused the two: everyone has the gene, and what differs is the **allele**.

visual.alt: A table of the three genotypes with their phenotypes: FF and Ff both look unaffected although their alleles differ, and only ff shows the condition

steps.title: The words you need
steps.body:
**The specification lists eleven terms and asks you to explain them.** Getting them exactly right is most of the marks in this topic.

**Chromosome** — a long molecule of DNA, carrying many genes.

**Gene** — a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.

**Allele** — a **different version of the same gene**. A gene for eye colour may have a brown allele and a blue allele.

**Dominant** — an allele that is **expressed even when only one copy is present**. Written as a **capital** letter.

**Recessive** — an allele expressed **only when two copies are present**. Written as a **lower case** letter.

**Homozygous** — having **two identical alleles** of a gene: `BB` or `bb`.

**Heterozygous** — having **two different alleles**: `Bb`.

**Genotype** — the **alleles** an organism has, such as `Bb`.

**Phenotype** — the **observable characteristic** that results, such as brown eyes.

**Gamete** — a sex cell, carrying **one allele** of each gene.

**Zygote** — the cell formed when **two gametes fuse** at fertilisation, carrying **two** alleles again.

**Why differences arise.** *There are differences in inherited characteristics as a result of alleles.* Two organisms differ because they carry **different versions of the same genes** — not different genes.

**The genotype–phenotype distinction is the one to master**, because `BB` and `Bb` give the **same phenotype** while being different genotypes. That is exactly why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

steps.title: Mendel
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **The specification asks you to describe the work of Gregor Mendel in discovering the basis of genetics, and to recognise the difficulties of understanding inheritance before the mechanism was discovered.**

**What Mendel did.** Working with **pea plants** in the nineteenth century, he studied characteristics with two clear alternatives — tall or short, round or wrinkled seeds. He **crossed plants carefully**, recorded the offspring over **several generations**, and — crucially — **counted them in large numbers**.

**What he found.** Characteristics were passed on as separate **units** that did not blend. A characteristic could **disappear** in one generation and **reappear** in the next, and the numbers came out in consistent **ratios** — notably **3 : 1**.

**Why that was so important.** It showed inheritance was governed by **discrete factors** — what we now call **alleles** — rather than by the offspring being a blend of its parents, which was the common assumption.

**Why he was not believed at the time.** This is the part the specification highlights. **DNA, chromosomes and genes had not yet been discovered**, so Mendel could describe the **pattern** without being able to explain the **mechanism**. He had no physical thing to point to.

His work was also **mathematical**, at a time when biology was largely descriptive, and it was published in an obscure journal.

**His work was only recognised decades later**, after it was rediscovered in 1900 and the behaviour of chromosomes during gamete formation was seen to match exactly what his ratios required. The discovery of the mechanism turned his patterns into an explanation.

**The wider point** is worth stating: a correct theory can be **ignored** when there is no known mechanism to support it, and later confirmed when the mechanism is found.

steps.title: Sex determination and pedigrees
steps.body:
**The sex of offspring is determined at fertilisation**, and the specification asks you to show it with a genetic diagram.

**Females are XX and males are XY.** A mother therefore produces gametes that all carry **X**. A father produces two kinds: half carry **X** and half carry **Y**.

**The Punnett square** gives **2 XX : 2 XY** — a **50% chance** of each sex at every conception.

**Note what this means.** It is the **father's gamete** that determines the sex, since the mother can only contribute an X. And the 50% applies **independently to each child** — a family of four girls does not make a boy more likely next time.

**Family pedigrees** trace a characteristic through several generations. By convention **squares are males** and **circles are females**, and shaded symbols show individuals with the characteristic.

**How to read one.** The key move is to look for a characteristic that **skips a generation** — appearing in a grandparent and a grandchild but not the parent in between. That means the characteristic is **recessive**, because the parent must have carried the allele without showing it, as a **heterozygous carrier**.

**If two unaffected parents have an affected child**, the characteristic must be **recessive** and both parents must be **heterozygous** — each passed on a recessive allele they did not show.

**Most characteristics are not this simple.** The specification notes that **most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance**. Height, skin colour and most of what makes people differ are controlled by many genes together, which is why they vary continuously rather than falling into two clear groups.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep genotype and phenotype apart.** **Genotype** is the **alleles**; **phenotype** is the **observable characteristic**. `BB` and `Bb` are different genotypes with the **same phenotype** — and that single fact explains almost every "how can this happen" question in genetics.

**Label the square before filling it.** Parent genotypes, then gametes on the top and side, then the boxes. The classic error is combining two alleles from the **same** parent, and labelling first makes it impossible.

**Recognise the standard crosses.** `Bb × Bb` → **3 : 1** (75% / 25%). `BB × bb` → **all heterozygous**, all showing the dominant characteristic. `Bb × bb` → **1 : 1**. Knowing these saves time and catches errors.

**Answer the "how can this happen" question properly.** Two parents showing the dominant characteristic can have a recessive child **only if both are heterozygous** — each passing on a recessive allele they carry but do not show. That gives the 25% chance, and it is the commonest six-mark question in this topic.

**Read pedigrees by looking for a skip.** A characteristic appearing in a grandparent and a grandchild but **not the parent between** must be **recessive**, and the parent must be a **heterozygous carrier**. Equally, **two unaffected parents with an affected child** proves the trait is recessive and both parents heterozygous.

**Treat ratios as probabilities per birth.** A 3 : 1 ratio is what is **expected** across many offspring, not a guarantee in any one family. Each child is an **independent** event — three affected children do not make a fourth less likely. Examiners test this directly.

*(Biology only.)* **Explain Mendel through the missing mechanism.** He established the **pattern** — discrete units, consistent ratios, characteristics skipping generations — but **DNA, chromosomes and genes were unknown**, so he could not say **what** was being inherited. His work was accepted decades later, once chromosomes were seen to behave exactly as his ratios required.

**Remember that most features are polygenic.** **Most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance.** Monohybrid crosses are a simplification chosen because they are tractable, not because most characteristics work that way.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **allele** is a **different version of the same gene**.
- **Dominant** alleles are expressed with **one copy** (capital letter); **recessive** need **two** (lower case).
- **Homozygous** = two identical alleles; **heterozygous** = two different.
- **Genotype** = the alleles; **phenotype** = the observable characteristic.
- `BB` and `Bb` are different genotypes with the **same phenotype**.
- A **gamete** carries **one** allele of each gene; a **zygote** has **two**.
- **Mendel** used **pea plants**, counted large numbers, and found **3 : 1** ratios.
- He showed inheritance is by **discrete units**, not blending.
- He was ignored because **genes and chromosomes were unknown** — a pattern with no mechanism.
- `Bb × Bb` gives **1 : 2 : 1** genotypes and **3 : 1** phenotypes (75% / 25%).
- `BB × bb` gives **all heterozygous**.
- Females are **XX**, males **XY**; the **father's gamete** decides the sex.
- Sex determination gives a **50%** chance of each, **independently** for each child.
- In a pedigree, a characteristic that **skips a generation** is **recessive**.
- **Most phenotypic features result from multiple genes**, not single gene inheritance.

questions.prompt: Two parents who both have brown eyes have a child with blue eyes. Brown (B) is dominant to blue (b). Explain how this is possible, using a genetic diagram, and give the probability of it happening again.
questions.solution:
**Start from the child.** Blue is **recessive**, and a recessive characteristic is expressed **only when two copies are present**. The blue-eyed child must therefore be **homozygous recessive**, with the genotype **bb**.

**Where those alleles came from.** The child received **one allele from each parent**, so **each parent must have passed on a recessive allele, b**.

But both parents have **brown** eyes, and brown is dominant. So neither can be `bb`. Each must have **at least one B** to show brown eyes, and **at least one b** to have passed one on. Both parents are therefore **heterozygous, Bb** — they each carry the blue allele without showing it.

**The genetic diagram.** Each `Bb` parent produces two kinds of gamete: **B** and **b**.

|  | **B** | **b** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **B** | BB | Bb |
| **b** | Bb | bb |

The four equally likely outcomes are **1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb**.

**Grouping by phenotype**, `BB` and `Bb` both show **brown** eyes, because one dominant allele is enough. Only `bb` shows **blue**. The phenotype ratio is therefore **3 brown : 1 blue**.

**The probability** of a blue-eyed child is **1 in 4**, or **25%**.

**What that probability means** matters as much as the number. It is the chance **at each conception**, and each birth is an **independent event**. If these parents have another child, the chance of blue eyes is **still 25%** — and it would remain 25% even if they already had three blue-eyed children. The ratio describes what is **expected on average over many offspring**, not a pattern that a single family is obliged to follow. A family of four children might have no blue-eyed child at all, or all four, without anything being wrong with the genetics.

This case also illustrates the distinction between **genotype** and **phenotype**. Both parents have the same **phenotype** as a `BB` individual would — brown eyes — but a different **genotype**, and it is the genotype that determines what they can pass on.

questions.prompt: Describe the work of Gregor Mendel and explain why his conclusions were not accepted until long after his death.
questions.solution:
**What Mendel did.** Working in the nineteenth century with **pea plants**, Gregor Mendel studied characteristics that came in **two clear alternatives** — tall or short plants, round or wrinkled seeds — so that every offspring could be placed unambiguously in one group or the other.

He **crossed plants deliberately and carefully**, controlling which plant pollinated which, and followed the offspring over **several generations**. Crucially, he **counted them in large numbers**, which meant that consistent proportions emerged from what would otherwise have looked like random variation.

**What he found.** Characteristics were **not blended** in the offspring. A tall plant crossed with a short one did not give medium plants; the offspring were tall or short. A characteristic could **disappear entirely in one generation and reappear in the next**, which blending could not explain at all.

When he counted, the numbers fell into consistent **ratios** — most famously **3 : 1** in the second generation.

**What he concluded.** Inheritance is governed by **separate, discrete units** passed from parent to offspring — what we now call **alleles**. Each parent contributes one of a pair, some versions **mask** others, and a masked version can still be passed on and reappear later. That explains both the disappearance and the reappearance, and it predicts the ratios he counted.

**Why he was not believed.** The central difficulty, which the specification highlights, is that Mendel could describe the **pattern** of inheritance but could not explain the **mechanism**. **DNA, chromosomes and genes had not yet been discovered**, so he had no physical structure to point to. He was proposing invisible "factors" whose existence rested entirely on the numbers, and asking biologists to accept something no one could observe.

Several things worked against him. His approach was **mathematical**, at a time when biology was overwhelmingly **descriptive**, so his methods were unfamiliar to his readers. The prevailing assumption was that offspring **blended** their parents' characteristics, and his conclusions contradicted it directly. His paper was also published in an **obscure journal** and read by very few people.

**How it was eventually accepted.** Decades later, after his work was **rediscovered in 1900**, biologists saw that **chromosomes behave during gamete formation** exactly as his ratios required — they occur in pairs, separate into gametes, and recombine at fertilisation. The mechanism had been found, and it fitted the pattern he had described precisely.

**The wider point** is worth drawing out: a correct explanation can be **ignored for decades** when there is no known mechanism to support it, and confirmed later when the mechanism is discovered. Mendel's work was not accepted because it was persuasive, but because the evidence eventually caught up with it.

Crucially, he **counted them in large numbers**, which meant that consistent proportions emerged from what would otherwise have looked like random variation.

**What he found.** Characteristics were **not blended** in the offspring. A tall plant crossed with a short one did not give medium plants; the offspring were tall or short. A characteristic could **disappear entirely in one generation and reappear in the next**, which blending could not explain at all.

When he counted, the numbers fell into consistent **ratios** — most famously **3 : 1** in the second generation.

**What he concluded.** Inheritance is governed by **separate, discrete units** passed from parent to offspring — what we now call **alleles**. Each parent contributes one of a pair, some versions **mask** others, and a masked version can still be passed on and reappear later. That explains both the disappearance and the reappearance, and it predicts the ratios he counted.

**Why he was not believed.** The central difficulty, which the specification highlights, is that Mendel could describe the **pattern** of inheritance but could not explain the **mechanism**. **DNA, chromosomes and genes had not yet been discovered**, so he had no physical structure to point to. He was proposing invisible "factors" whose existence rested entirely on the numbers, and asking biologists to accept something no one could observe.

Several things worked against him. His approach was **mathematical**, at a time when biology was overwhelmingly **descriptive**, so his methods were unfamiliar to his readers. The prevailing assumption was that offspring **blended** their parents' characteristics, and his conclusions contradicted it directly. His paper was also published in an **obscure journal** and read by very few people.

**How it was eventually accepted.** Decades later, after his work was **rediscovered in 1900**, biologists saw that **chromosomes behave during gamete formation** exactly as his ratios required — they occur in pairs, separate into gametes, and recombine at fertilisation. The mechanism had been found, and it fitted the pattern he had described precisely.

**The wider point** is worth drawing out: a correct explanation can be **ignored for decades** when there is no known mechanism to support it, and confirmed later when the mechanism is discovered. Mendel's work was not accepted because it was persuasive, but because the evidence eventually caught up with it.

questions.prompt: In guinea pigs, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant to the allele for white fur (b). A heterozygous black guinea pig (Bb) is crossed with a white guinea pig (bb). What percentage of the offspring are expected to have white fur?
questions.solution: The Bb parent gives gametes **B** and **b**; the bb parent gives only **b**. The square holds **Bb, Bb, bb, bb**, so 2 of the 4 offspring are **bb** and white: **50%**. This is the **1 : 1** ratio of a heterozygous × homozygous recessive cross.

markScheme.description: gametes B and b, with b only; offspring 2 Bb : 2 bb

questions.prompt:
A condition is controlled by a single gene. The table describes one family.

| Person | Parents | Shows the condition? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mother | not known | no |
| Father | not known | no |
| Daughter | Mother and Father | yes |
| Son | Mother and Father | no |

The mother and father have another child. What is the percentage chance that this child is a carrier: heterozygous, without showing the condition?
questions.solution: The daughter shows the condition but **neither parent does**, so the allele must be **recessive** and each parent must carry one copy without showing it: both are **Aa**. The cross Aa × Aa gives **AA, Aa, Aa, aa**. The carriers are the two **Aa** boxes, so the chance is 2 in 4, or **50%**. The unaffected son does not change this, because each birth is independent.

markScheme.description: deduces the condition is recessive and both parents are heterozygous
Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa

questions.prompt: What is a zygote?
questions.solution: **The cell formed when a male and a female gamete fuse** at fertilisation. It carries two alleles of each gene again, one from each gamete. A sex cell with half the number of chromosomes is a **gamete**; an organism with two different alleles of a gene is **heterozygous**; and a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein is a **gene**.

markScheme.description: the cell formed when a male and a female gamete fuse

options: A sex cell with half the normal number of chromosomes
The cell formed when a male and a female gamete fuse
An organism with two different alleles of one gene
A section of DNA that codes for one specific protein

questions.prompt: A brother and sister have the same two parents, but they show different forms of a characteristic that is controlled by a single gene. Why?
questions.solution: **Each inherited a different combination of the parents' alleles.** Each parent has two alleles of the gene and passes only one of them, at random, in each gamete. So two children of the same parents can receive different alleles, giving different genotypes and so different phenotypes. Every child inherits one set of chromosomes from each parent, each with one copy of the gene, and alleles are passed on whole: they do not blend.

markScheme.description: each inherited a different combination of the parents' alleles

options: Each inherited a different combination of the parents' alleles
One of them inherited all of their genes from only one parent
One of them has more copies of the gene than the other one does
Their parents' alleles blended together in a different way in each

questions.prompt: Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall pea plants with pure-breeding short pea plants, and all the offspring were tall. When he crossed these tall offspring with each other, about one in four of the next generation was short, and none was of in-between height. What did the return of the short plants suggest?
questions.solution: **The factor for shortness had been passed on unchanged, hidden by the tall one.** The first offspring were all tall, yet they produced short plants, so they must have been carrying the factor for shortness without showing it. It came back exactly as it was, not diluted, so inheritance was by separate units that do not blend: what we now call **alleles**, with tall dominant to short. The plants were not in-between, which rules out blending. A new factor appearing in one plant could not give a steady one in four across a whole generation. Poor soil in one generation could not explain the same one in four appearing whenever such plants were crossed.

markScheme.description: the factor for shortness was passed on unchanged, hidden by the tall factor

options: The short plants had been stunted by poor soil in the second generation
The factor for shortness had been passed on unchanged, hidden by the tall one
The tall and short factors had blended, giving plants of in-between height
Shortness was a new factor, created by a change in the second generation

questions.prompt: In mice, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant to the allele for brown fur (b). A breeder crosses a black mouse of unknown genotype with a brown mouse (bb). Of the 7 offspring, 3 have brown fur. What does this show about the black parent?
questions.solution: **It is Bb.** A brown mouse has genotype bb, so each brown offspring must have received a b allele from **each** parent. The brown parent can only pass on b, so the black parent must also carry b: it is **Bb**. A BB parent could only pass on B, so every offspring would be Bb and black. A black mouse cannot be bb, because bb gives brown fur. The litter of 3 brown to 4 black is close to the 1 : 1 expected from Bb × bb, but it is the brown offspring themselves that prove the genotype, not the ratio.

markScheme.description: it is Bb, because each brown offspring received a b allele from it

options: It is BB, because more than half of the offspring have black fur like it
It is bb, because only two brown parents can have brown offspring
It is Bb, because each brown offspring received a b allele from it
It is BB, because a BB parent can pass on a b allele to some offspring

questions.prompt: Give the term for an organism that has two different alleles of a particular gene.
questions.solution: **Heterozygous**, such as `Bb`. An organism with two identical alleles, `BB` or `bb`, is **homozygous**. In a heterozygous organism with a dominant and a recessive allele, the dominant allele is expressed and the recessive one is hidden, but it can still be passed on in half of the gametes.

markScheme.description: heterozygous

questions.prompt: In pea plants, the allele for tall stems (T) is dominant to the allele for short stems (t). Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed, and 480 of the seeds produced grow into plants. Calculate the number of these plants expected to be tall.
questions.solution:
Each parent's gametes carry **T** or **t**. The Punnett square for Tt × Tt gives **TT, Tt, Tt, tt**. TT and Tt both have a T, so three of the four boxes are tall: 3 in 4, or 75%.

Expected tall plants = 480 × 3 ÷ 4 = **360**.

Check: the short plants are 480 ÷ 4 = 120, and 360 + 120 = 480.

markScheme.description: uses the cross to find that 3 in 4 (75%) are tall

questions.prompt: A condition is caused by a recessive allele (f) of a gene that is not on a sex chromosome; the dominant allele (F) does not cause it. Two parents who do not have the condition have a son who has it. A child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl, and sex does not affect this gene. Calculate the percentage chance that their next child will be a girl who has the condition.
questions.solution:
**The parents' genotypes.** The son has the condition, so he is **ff** and received an f from each parent. Neither parent has the condition, so each also has an F: both are **Ff**.

**The condition.** Ff × Ff: each parent's gametes carry F or f, giving **FF, Ff, Ff, ff**. Only ff has the condition, so the chance is 1 in 4.

**The sex.** The mother is XX and her eggs all carry X; the father is XY and his sperm carry X or Y. The cross gives **XX, XX, XY, XY**, so the chance of a girl is 1 in 2.

**Both together.** The two are independent, so multiply: $\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}$, and 1 ÷ 8 × 100 = **12.5%**.

markScheme.description: deduces that both parents are Ff, so the chance of ff is 1 in 4
multiplies by the chance of a girl, 1 in 2

questions.prompt: In Mendel's pea plants, stem height was controlled by a single gene, and the plants were either tall or short. Human height is different: adults show a continuous range of heights rather than a few separate groups. Explain why.
questions.solution: Most phenotypic features, human height among them, are the result of **multiple genes** rather than a single gene. Each gene has its own alleles, so there are a great many possible **combinations**, each shifting height a little, and the heights form a continuous range. The environment, such as diet, adds further variation.

markScheme.description: human height is the result of multiple genes rather than a single gene
any valid link to the continuous range (e.g. the many combinations of alleles of these genes give many small differences, or the environment, such as diet, adds further variation)

criteria.text: States that human height is the result of multiple genes rather than a single gene
Gives any valid link to the continuous range (e.g. the many combinations of alleles of these genes give many small differences in height, or the environment, such as diet, adds further variation)

questions.modelAnswer: A single gene with a dominant and a recessive allele gives only a few genotypes, and so only two clear phenotypes, which is why Mendel's plants were either tall or short. Human height, like most phenotypic features, is the result of multiple genes rather than a single gene. Each of these genes has its own alleles, and each allele adds or takes away a little height, so the number of possible combinations is very large. The combinations differ from each other by small amounts, so the heights in a population merge into a continuous range instead of separate groups. The environment, such as diet during childhood, adds further variation on top of this.

questions.prompt: In a large population, about half of all babies born are boys and half are girls. Using the sex chromosomes of each parent, their gametes and fertilisation, explain why. You may use a genetic diagram.
questions.solution:
A female is **XX**, so every egg carries an **X**. A male is **XY**, so half of his sperm carry an **X** and half carry a **Y**. At fertilisation an egg is equally likely to be fertilised by either kind:

| | X sperm | Y sperm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X egg | XX girl | XY boy |
| X egg | XX girl | XY boy |

Two boxes in four are girls and two are boys, a 1 : 1 ratio, so each baby has a 50% chance of being a boy.

markScheme.description: females are XX, so every egg carries an X chromosome
males are XY, so half the sperm carry an X and half a Y
an egg is equally likely to be fertilised by an X or a Y sperm, giving XX girls and XY boys in a 1 : 1 ratio

criteria.text: States that females are XX, so every egg carries an X chromosome
States that males are XY, so half of the sperm carry an X chromosome and half carry a Y
Explains that at fertilisation an egg is equally likely to be fertilised by an X or a Y sperm, giving XX (girl) or XY (boy) in a 1 : 1 ratio, a 50% chance of each

questions.modelAnswer: Sex is decided by one pair of chromosomes, the sex chromosomes. A female is XX. When her eggs are made, each egg receives one of her sex chromosomes, and since both are X, every egg carries an X. A male is XY. When his sperm are made, each sperm receives one of his two sex chromosomes, so half of the sperm carry an X and half carry a Y. At fertilisation, an egg is equally likely to be fertilised by an X sperm or a Y sperm. An X sperm gives an XX zygote, which develops into a girl; a Y sperm gives an XY zygote, which develops into a boy. A genetic diagram of XX × XY gives XX, XX, XY and XY, two girls to two boys, a 1 : 1 ratio. So each baby has a 50% chance of being a boy, and across a large population about half are boys and half are girls.

questions.prompt:
A condition is caused by a dominant allele, D; the recessive allele, d, does not cause it. The gene is not on a sex chromosome. The table describes one family.

| Person | Parents | Has the condition? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grandmother | not known | yes |
| Grandfather | not known | no |
| Ann | Grandmother and Grandfather | yes |
| Ben | Grandmother and Grandfather | no |
| Carl, Ann's partner | not known | no |
| Dee, Ben's partner | not known | no |

Use genetic diagrams to work out the chance that a child of Ann and Carl will have the condition, and the chance that a child of Ben and Dee will have it. Explain why Ben cannot pass the condition on, even though his mother has it.
questions.solution:
**Genotypes.** D is dominant, so one copy causes the condition. Everyone without it must be **dd**: the grandfather, Ben, Carl and Dee. Ann has the condition, so she has at least one D, and she received a d from her dd father, so she is **Dd**.

**Ann × Carl, Dd × dd.** Ann's gametes carry D or d; Carl's all carry d.

| | D | d |
| --- | --- | --- |
| d | Dd | dd |
| d | Dd | dd |

Two boxes in four are Dd: a **50%** chance for each child.

**Ben × Dee, dd × dd.** Every gamete carries d, so every child is dd: a **0%** chance.

**Why Ben cannot pass it on.** He received d from his mother, not D, and a single D would have given him the condition. With no D in his genotype, none of his gametes can carry it. A dominant allele cannot be carried hidden.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): gives some correct genotypes, such as dd for the people without the condition, or a correct chance for one couple, with little reasoning
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): deduces the genotypes and works out at least one couple's chance from a genetic diagram, but misses a link, such as why Ann must be Dd, or why Ben cannot pass the allele on

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): deduces that everyone without the condition is dd and that Ann is Dd because her father gave her d; shows Dd × dd giving 50% and dd × dd giving 0%; and explains that Ben has no D allele, so none of his gametes can carry it

criteria.text: States that everyone without the condition (the grandfather, Ben, Carl and Dee) must be dd, because a single D allele would cause it
Deduces that Ann is Dd: she has the condition, so has a D, and she received a d from her dd father
Shows the cross Dd × dd with its gametes (D or d from Ann, d only from Carl) and offspring Dd, Dd, dd, dd
Concludes a 50% (1 in 2) chance for each child of Ann and Carl
Shows that dd × dd gives only dd, so a 0% chance for a child of Ben and Dee
Explains that Ben received d, not D, from his mother, so he has no D allele and none of his gametes can carry it

questions.modelAnswer:
**The genotypes.** D is dominant, so a single copy is enough to cause the condition. Anyone who does not have it cannot have any D: the grandfather, Ben, Carl and Dee are all **dd**. Ann has the condition, so she has at least one D. Her father is dd and could only give her d, so Ann is **Dd**. (The grandmother must be Dd too, since she had Ben, who is dd.)

**Ann and Carl.** Dd × dd. Ann's gametes carry D or d, equally often; Carl's all carry d.

| | D (Ann) | d (Ann) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| d (Carl) | Dd | dd |
| d (Carl) | Dd | dd |

Two of the four equally likely outcomes are Dd, so each child has a **50%** (1 in 2) chance of having the condition. That chance is the same for every child, whatever happened to earlier ones.

**Ben and Dee.** dd × dd. Every gamete from both parents carries d, so every child is dd: a **0%** chance.

**Why Ben cannot pass it on.** Ben's mother is Dd, and each of her children had an equal chance of receiving D or d from her. Ben received **d**; if he had received D he would have the condition himself. So Ben has no D allele at all, and an allele that is not in his genotype cannot be in any of his gametes. Unlike a recessive allele, a dominant allele cannot be carried hidden by someone who does not show it, so the condition cannot pass down Ben's side of the family.

examTechnique.body:
Keep **genotype** (the alleles) apart from **phenotype** (the appearance) — `BB` and `Bb` look the same. **Label the gametes** on a Punnett square before filling it.

Learn the standard results: `Bb × Bb` → **3 : 1**, `BB × bb` → **all heterozygous**. Treat every ratio as a **probability per birth**, not a guarantee.
examinerErrors: Using genotype and phenotype as if they meant the same.
Combining two alleles from the same parent in a Punnett square.
Giving the genotype ratio when the phenotype ratio was asked for.
Saying previous children change the probability for the next.
Failing to deduce that both parents must be heterozygous.
Assuming all characteristics are controlled by a single gene.
Forgetting that the father's gamete determines sex.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates **genotype** from **phenotype** and uses that distinction to explain how a recessive characteristic reappears. It **labels the gametes** before filling a Punnett square, gives the **phenotype** ratio when asked for it, and deduces parents' genotypes by reasoning **backwards from the child**. It treats a ratio as a **probability for each birth**, stating explicitly that previous children change nothing. On Mendel it credits him with the **pattern** rather than with genes, and explains his neglect through the **missing mechanism** — chromosomes and DNA were unknown — and his rehabilitation once chromosomes were seen to behave as his ratios demanded. It also remembers that **most features are polygenic**.
